insight.title: Short Videos Made 10 Seconds Feel Long
insight.subtitle: Our tolerance for setup has vanished, turning even brief clips into tests of patience.

sections.text: Notice how fast your thumb moves if a short clip takes three seconds to get to the point? A tiny setup now feels like an unskippable pre-roll ad.
Short-form feeds have eliminated the concept of an introduction. When every video starts mid-action, basic context starts to look like wasted time.
The result isn't just shorter attention spans; it's a new demand for hyper-edited reality. We now expect real-world stories to cut straight to the punchline.
If a clip needs an intro, you've already swiped.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is today's news explained plainly and simply.

Officials from Ukraine, Russia, and the United States meet in Abu Dhabi this week for peace talks. This is the fourth round of talks in 2026 to end the war. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner head the United States delegation. Foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov leads the Ukrainian team. Former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky leads the Russian side. President Donald Trump urged Ukraine to give up territory for a peace deal. The Kremlin said European officials will not be part of the meetings. An EU official said representatives from Europe will be on site, but their role is unclear. Russia currently occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine. The talks are scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.

Turning to technology, United States tech stocks dropped sharply this week after weeks of declines. The S&P 500 technology sector recorded its biggest single-day fall in more than six years. Technology shares make up more than 35 percent of the main United States stock index. Despite recent losses, Sandisk shares remained up around 250 percent in 2026. Dell shares were up around 160 percent, and Micron gained around 140 percent. On Thursday, the technology sector price-to-earnings ratio fell to 17 point 1. The ratio for the broader market stood at 17 point 9. This was the first time since 2017 that tech stocks became cheaper than the market. Investors are watching the planned public stock offering of artificial intelligence company Anthropic.

In global news, leaders from nearly 200 countries gathered in Turkey on Monday for a climate summit. The United Nations summit called COP31 will run for two weeks in Antalya. The UN warned the world is almost certain to pass the warming limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius. The United States is not attending the climate talks. The meeting comes during the strongest El Nino weather system on record. This weather system is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives. It is also expected to cause damage costing trillions of dollars. At a past summit, host country Brazil said national governments must handle emission cuts. The summit aims to remove obstacles that are slowing down decarbonization efforts.

In agricultural news, a flesh-eating parasite has spread across Mexico into the United States. The pest, called the screwworm, broke through a barrier in Panama in early 2023. Officials release factory-bred sterile flies to stop the parasite from reproducing. Mexico and Panama currently produce about 150 million sterile flies per week. Experts recommend 500 million flies per week to keep the pest contained. The United States closed its border to Mexican cattle imports for more than 15 months. Mexico has recorded about 51,000 cases of the pest in livestock. The United States has confirmed 120 cases to date. A new fly production facility in Texas will not start operating until spring 2027.

Over in legal news, Chinese technology company Huawei is on trial in Brooklyn, New York. Huawei is the largest telecommunications equipment maker in the world. United States prosecutors accuse Huawei of stealing technology from American companies. They also accuse the firm of breaking sanctions by trading with Iran and North Korea. In 2018, Canadian authorities arrested Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou. China then detained two Canadian citizens for nearly three years in response. A United States plea deal later freed Meng and released the two Canadians. Signed admissions from Meng have now been read aloud to the Brooklyn jury. The jury will decide if Huawei broke laws on fraud, theft, and sanctions.

Moving to financial news, the International Monetary Fund began reviewing Ukraine's lending program on Monday. The International Monetary Fund provides financial aid to countries in need. This official review could unlock about 1 point 6 7 billion dollars for Ukraine. Ukraine faces a funding gap of about 70 billion dollars next year. Ukraine's economy shrank by 0 point 7 percent in the third quarter of this year. The central bank expects the economy to drop 0 point 4 percent in 2026. Inflation in Ukraine is expected to reach 12 point 5 percent this year. Ukrainian officials and financial teams are meeting in Lviv and Warsaw for the review.

Next, companies risk fines of six percent global turnover for unfair digital trade practices, EU draft law shows.

A proposed European Union law could fine companies up to six percent of global turnover. The fines target companies using unfair digital trade practices to push purchases or target children. European Commission Justice chief Michael McGrath will present the Digital Fairness Act on Wednesday. The law would ban manipulative app designs that steer people into buying more items. It would also ban personalized advertising aimed at children or vulnerable consumers. Companies using dynamic pricing must disclose how many items exist at advertised prices. Traders must let users switch off addictive features that encourage excessive use. Advocacy group Finance Watch says the draft does not fully protect online financial investors. The proposal needs approval from European Union countries and the European Parliament.

Turning to technology news, Google warned an Australian bill could block under-eighteens from Gmail. Australia is considering a bill to force companies to remove harmful online content. Companies facing violations could pay fines up to one hundred nine million Australian dollars. Google policy head Rachel Lord spoke at a Senate hearing on Monday. She said age checks might force platforms to block minors from email and file storage. She added that this could lead to intrusive monitoring within private communications. Representatives from Meta, TikTok, and Snap also warned regulators would get too much discretion. The Australian government says broad rules are necessary to keep the internet safe. The Senate hearing is continuing.

In economic news, the Philippine economy grew by two point one percent in the third quarter. That is a fifth straight quarter of slowing growth for the country. A poll by Reuters had expected growth of three percent. Household spending and government consumption both slowed down during the quarter. Agricultural output fell four point eight percent after growing in the previous quarter. Inflation reached seven point eight percent in October due to food and fuel costs. Economic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said full-year growth may miss government targets. Infrastructure spending fell fifteen point one percent amid a flood control corruption scandal. The central bank raised interest rates by one hundred twenty-five basis points since April.

Next, researchers solved a mystery about electrical power grids dropping frequency every sixty seconds worldwide. Transmission operator Tennet Germany brought the issue to researcher Dirk Witthaut in Germany. Frequency drops occurred every minute across grids in Europe, Australia, and the United States. Unchecked frequency drops can damage equipment in power plants or cause wide blackouts. Researchers placed more than eighty power meters around their campus to trace the issue. They discovered stationary battery backup systems check their charge levels every minute. Because these batteries connect to the internet, their internal clocks check at the same time. Data center batteries in Ireland caused frequency drops to quadruple over five years. Researchers say this grid disruption is entirely preventable.

Moving to international news, a barrier failure at a major hydropower project caused flooding in Pakistan. A protective barrier collapsed at the partially constructed Tarbela Dam T-five hydropower project. The collapse of the protective barrier caused a surge of flood water.

In science news, NASA has opened a new recruitment drive for upcoming lunar missions. The space agency is looking for astronauts to live and work on the Moon. NASA needs more recruits in order to return to the Moon. The agency has been away from the Moon for more than half a century.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Short-form video feeds have changed how quickly people expect content to get to the point. When clips start mid-action, even a three-second setup feels like an unskippable ad. Basic context in a video can now look like wasted time to viewers. This shift has created a strong demand for hyper-edited reality. People now expect real-world stories to cut straight to the punchline right away. If a clip takes time to set up, most viewers have already swiped away. It is interesting how brief videos have transformed our patience for simple introductions. When you watch a video today, how many seconds will you give it before moving on?

Thank you for tuning in to the Sift Daily Briefing, and stay curious until next time.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is our full analysis, giving you the complete story behind today's headlines.

What can we expect from the new peace talks between Russia, the US, and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi? Officials are meeting to try to end the war, but analysts expect very little progress.

Nearly five years ago, Russia launched a war against Ukraine. Before that, Russia annexed the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea in 2014. The United Nations does not recognize that takeover. Russia now occupies roughly twenty percent of Ukraine, including parts of the eastern Donbas region. The war has killed thousands of people and displaced millions. Ukraine wants Russia to withdraw entirely from its land. Ukraine also wants strong security guarantees to prevent future attacks. However, Russia refuses to end its occupation. Russia demands that Ukraine never join the NATO alliance, which is a Western military group. Russia also opposes foreign troops being placed in Ukraine after any deal. The two sides held three rounds of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year. However, no meeting has come close to a breakthrough since March 2022 in Istanbul.

US President Donald Trump recently pushed to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two. Trump claimed the war was close to being settled. However, he also blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for holding up peace efforts. The US also signed a deal last month to buy Russian diesel, giving Moscow extra revenue.

Now, officials are meeting in Abu Dhabi for two days of negotiations. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner head the American delegation. Ukraine foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov leads Kyiv's team, along with chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky leads the Russian group. US envoy Jared Kushner outlined four main priorities for these talks. They are stopping the fighting, creating security guarantees, funding economic recovery, and returning prisoners. European security officials from France, Germany, Britain, NATO, and the EU are also on site.

This meeting is the first direct three-way talk in nine months. It takes place as tit-for-tat attacks on energy sites have intensified in recent months.

Analysts say Ukraine's very independence and sovereignty are at stake. Giving up land or military choices would be very hard for Ukraine to accept. Analysts warn that a weak deal could threaten other post-Soviet states like Moldova, Georgia, and Belarus. Listeners should watch whether Russia shows any willingness to negotiate, or if it insists on full Ukrainian surrender.

Now, let's turn to the financial markets, where technology stocks are driving big swings on Wall Street.

Why are stock market investors closely watching artificial intelligence shares right now? A recent sell-off in technology stocks has created worry across the broader financial markets.

In October 2022, a major US stock market bull run began. Tech companies invested massive amounts of money into artificial intelligence, or AI. Running complex AI models requires huge computer facilities called data centers. Companies building this infrastructure saw their stock prices rise sharply. Tech shares gained more than two hundred percent over this period. That was nearly double the gain of the overall S&P 500 index. The S&P 500 tracks the performance of major US companies. Technology grew to make up over thirty-five percent of that total index. That is higher than the level seen during the internet bubble peak in 2000. Non-tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta also spent heavily on data centers. Some AI beneficiaries made huge gains. Shares of Sandisk remained up around two hundred fifty percent in 2026. Dell Technologies was up around one hundred sixty percent, and Micron gained around one hundred forty percent.

Technology and AI stocks began falling nearly a month ago. The decline reached a low point when the tech sector suffered its biggest single-day fall in six years.

US stocks recovered some losses on Monday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose one point two percent. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite each gained zero point eight percent. Brent crude oil prices dropped over four percent to ninety-four dollars and twenty-three cents a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate crude fell nearly four percent to eighty-seven dollars and twenty-six cents. Prices fell after President Donald Trump played down potential new military strikes on Iran. Meanwhile, the tech sector forward price-to-earnings ratio fell to seventeen point one. That fell below the broader market ratio of seventeen point nine for the first time since 2017.

Investors face a critical week of financial events. Cloud firm CoreWeave reports earnings on Tuesday, while chipmaker Nvidia reports on November 17. AI company Anthropic is also preparing for a potential initial public offering, or IPO, next week. Investors are also waiting for Tuesday's Consumer Price Index report to check US inflation levels.

Lower valuation ratios mean bad news might already be priced into tech stocks. Keith Lerner from Truist Advisory Services says even a little good news could now boost shares. However, if inflation stays high, the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and could harm stock valuations. Watch whether upcoming earnings from Nvidia and CoreWeave show that demand for AI tech remains strong.

Next, we look at global climate negotiations taking place against a backdrop of war and rising energy demand.

Can world leaders agree on concrete steps to slow global warming at the latest UN climate summit? Representatives from nearly two hundred countries are meeting, but geopolitical conflicts and waning ambition threaten progress.

In 2015, world leaders met in France and created the Paris climate agreement. They set a target to limit global warming to one point five degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Exceeding that threshold risks catastrophic climate disruptions. However, countries continued burning fossil fuels, causing greenhouse gas emissions to rise. Earth experienced severe heatwaves, droughts, and floods. A glacier collapse in Nepal recently triggered a flood that killed over fourteen hundred fifty people. A powerful El Nino weather pattern supercharged global temperatures even further. The United Nations Environment Programme warned in October that the world will overshoot the one point five degree limit. This year is now on track to be one of the four hottest years ever recorded.

The annual two-week UN climate summit, known as COP31, officially opened on Monday in Antalya, Turkey.

Turkey's COP31 President Murat Kurum urged nations to sign a new pledge. The pledge aims to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035. Currently, electricity powers only about one fifth of the global economy. UN Climate Executive Secretary Simon Stiell warned that current progress is nowhere near fast enough. He stressed that fossil fuel costs have spread inflation like a cancer. However, the United States is shunning the conference for a second straight year under President Donald Trump. Trump has encouraged policies that maximize US oil, gas, and coal production.

The summit happens as multiple global crises compete for attention. The nine-month war in Iran has disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. High fuel prices prompted countries like South Korea, India, and Thailand to burn more coal. Furthermore, the rapid growth of artificial intelligence is creating a surge in power demand, raising emissions further.

Climate advocates criticize Turkey's electrification pledge because it does not require electricity to come from clean sources. Australia's negotiation president Chris Bowen urged leaders to prove that international cooperation still works. Listeners should watch whether countries turn paper promises into real action, or if war and energy demands derail progress.

That brings us to our next story, about how the United States was left exposed to the flesh-eating screwworm.

How did the United States and Mexico let a flesh-eating parasite slip past their defenses? 
The United States is now scrambling to build a sterile-fly factory after years of delays and political holdups left the country exposed to a severe screwworm outbreak. 

For decades, planes dropped billions of factory-bred sterile flies to keep the flesh-eating New World screwworm out of North America’s cattle. This trick works because sterile males mate with wild females, so their eggs fail to hatch. But the strategy only works if the supply of flies never runs short. 

The parasite broke through a barrier of sterile flies in Panama in early 2023. At that point, the region lacked the capacity to contain it. Panama declared an emergency in July 2023. The administration of former US President Joe Biden announced nearly one hundred ten million dollars in December 2023 for detection and fly production. 

Political transitions and funding delays slowed down the response in Mexico. Outgoing officials warned their successors in September 2024. Early planning focused on converting an existing fruit-fly plant in Metapa, instead of building a new one. This handover delayed the effort by three to four months. 

Today, the situation has turned into a major crisis. Short on flies, the administration of US President Donald Trump closed the border with Mexico to cattle imports for more than fifteen months starting in May 2025. As the border began to reopen this year, dozens of cases were confirmed in US cattle. Mexico and Panama currently produce a total of about one hundred fifty million sterile flies a week. That is less than a third of the five hundred million per week it took during a nineteen sixties campaign that eradicated the screwworm in the United States. 

Meanwhile, the parasite has spread across most of Mexico with about fifty-one thousand confirmed cases. The United States has recorded one hundred twenty cases to date. The US has no sterile-fly plant of its own. 

Why is this happening at this moment? The parasite has ripped through Mexico and into the United States, forcing officials to rush production facilities. 

What does this mean for you, and what comes next? The outbreak threatens cattle supplies and cross-border trade. You should watch for the completion of the new plant in Texas, which the Trump administration awarded a six hundred ten million dollar contract to M.A. Mortenson to construct. Administration officials pressed to move faster, and a new timeline expects the plant to start production by April first of next year. 

That leads us to our next question. Why is the world's largest telecommunications company on trial in a New York courtroom? 
Huawei is facing a high-stakes federal trial because prosecutors accuse the Chinese firm of stealing American technology and evading sanctions. 

Huawei is a Chinese firm that makes smartphones, laptops, routers and all sorts of telecoms equipment. The United States has long alleged that Huawei products pose a security risk. U.S. prosecutors allege that Huawei built its telecoms empire by stealing from American companies and violated U.S. sanctions by doing business in Iran and North Korea. 

In twenty eighteen, this came to a head when Canadian authorities arrested Meng Wanzhou, the chief financial officer of Huawei. In what is widely seen as an act of retaliation, China arrested two Canadians living in China, including analyst Michael Kovrig, detaining them for nearly three years. The United States later agreed to a deal that freed Meng and released the two Canadians. 

Today, Huawei is on trial in a federal courtroom in Brooklyn. The jury is going to determine whether Huawei broke American laws on fraud, theft and sanctions violations. The jury has already heard from sixty-one prosecution witnesses. Now Huawei is starting to present its defense. 

Why is this happening now? The case comes after years of investigation and a high-profile prisoner swap that cleared the way for the legal proceedings to move forward in the United States. 

What does this mean for the listener? Prosecutors say Huawei deceived banks in moving money through the financial system and took technology from American companies. The trial puts evidence on the public record, tested by Huawei's own lawyers and decided by a jury of citizens. Huawei dismisses the accusations, calling them a smattering of isolated cases. The Chinese government calls the trial an example of U.S. economic bullying. You should watch for the jury's verdict, which will help governments decide whether Huawei can be trusted as a provider of critical telecom infrastructure equipment. 

Moving to our final story for today: how much money could Ukraine unlock from the International Monetary Fund? 
The International Monetary Fund has started a review of Ukraine's lending programme that could unlock one point sixty-seven billion dollars for Kyiv. 

Ukraine's economy has been battered by more than four years of war. As the conflict with Russia grinds on, Kyiv faces a multi-billion financing shortfall for next year. Cooperation with the IMF, Ukraine's key international lender, is critical to ensure funding from other partners and help maintain economic stability. 

Today, Priscilla Toffano, the IMF's resident representative in Ukraine, said discussions will cover macroeconomic and fiscal policies, as well as key structural reforms. Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said the meetings will also cover the budget and international financial aid for twenty twenty-seven. The review combines the second and third assessments of Ukraine's four-year IMF programme. 

The economy slipped into contraction this year. Gross domestic product was down by zero-point-seven percent year-on-year in the third quarter. The central bank expects GDP to slip by zero-point-four percent in twenty twenty-six. Inflation is on the rise and expected to reach twelve-point-five percent this year. Exports via the Black Sea ports are blocked, and main exporting sectors like agribusiness and the steel industry are crippled. Budget revenues are falling below the plan, leaving the country facing a massive funding gap of about seventy billion dollars next year. 

The central bank said that the IMF's team and Ukrainian officials will hold meetings in Lviv and Warsaw, with some experts joining online. 

Why is this happening right now? Ukraine is struggling to shore up its war-hit economy and plug a looming funding gap as intensified Russian air bombardments target businesses, energy infrastructure and revenue-generating sectors. 

What does this mean for you, and what should you watch next? The review could secure vital money to keep Ukraine's economy afloat. You should watch for the conclusion of these meetings to see if the funds are successfully disbursed to Kyiv. 

Companies risk fines of six percent global turnover for unfair digital trade practices, EU draft law shows.

Can companies be fined six percent of their global earnings for tricking people into buying things online?
Yes, according to a European Commission draft law seen by Reuters, companies could face fines as high as six percent of their annual global turnover for unfair digital trade practices.
For many years, the European Union has tried to control how big technology and social media companies treat users.
Europe is a group of countries that makes shared rules for businesses.
These countries want to stop websites from tricking people or hurting children.
Because of this history, the European Commission keeps writing new rules to police content on digital platforms.
Then the European Commission created a new draft law.
This proposed legislation is known as the Digital Fairness Act.
Michael McGrath, who is the Commission's Justice chief, will present the proposed legislation on Wednesday.
The new draft law still needs to be thrashed out with European Union countries and the European Parliament before it can become law.
The draft law would ban business to consumer dark patterns.
Dark patterns are deceptive or manipulative interface designs on websites and apps.
They steer people into buying more, so the document calls them unfair commercial practices.
The Commission also wants to ban personalised advertising targeting children or vulnerable consumers.
Companies use dynamic pricing, where ticket prices fluctuate based on real-time demand.
This practice has triggered criticism from consumers.
So the law will require companies to be more transparent by disclosing the number of items available at the advertised price.
Traders will also have to give users the opportunity to switch off addictive features that encourage compulsive or excessive use.
Finance Watch is a group that campaigns for the public interest in financial services rulemaking.
According to Peter Norwood, who is a senior research and advocacy officer at Finance Watch, the proposed legislation does not do enough to protect consumers investing online.
Peter Norwood said that the proposals on dark patterns go in the right direction, but they lack ambition to sufficiently protect consumers in financial services.
This is happening now because Europe continues its latest legislative push to get big tech, e-commerce and social media giants to do more to police content on their platforms.
For the listener, this could mean websites change how they look and sell things if the law passes.
You might see fewer tricks online and more choices to turn off addictive features.
You should watch to see how European countries and the European Parliament change the draft law before it becomes final.
Now let us look at what is happening with internet rules in Australia.

Could a new internet safety law in Australia cut off children from using Gmail?
Yes, a proposed Australian internet law could force Google to block under-eighteen-year-olds from using its Gmail service, according to an Australia-based company policy head.
Over the years, internet companies grew very large and connected billions of people.
Governments around the world started to worry about children seeing bad things online.
So, lawmakers began writing rules to make online platforms responsible for keeping users safe.
Then Australia created the Digital Duty of Care legislation.
This law has already passed Australia's House of Representatives, but it still needs cross-party support to pass the Senate.
Under this law, internet companies must show they are taking steps to weed out harmful content.
If they do not, they face a fine of up to one hundred nine million Australian dollars, which is seventy-five point one million US dollars.
Online companies and free speech advocates say the law gives regulators too much discretion to decide what is harmful.
This discretion places pressure on platforms to take down content.
Google warned that the law could filter into everyday parts of the internet.
At a Senate hearing, Rachel Lord spoke about the risk.
Rachel Lord is the head of policy in Australia and New Zealand for Google's YouTube streaming website.
She said a section of the law requires age checks if there is a risk of a child seeing pornography.
She stated that this rule could require Google to age assure and block access to everyday communication services like messaging, email and private file storage.
She added that we are talking about potentially intrusive monitoring within private communications or file storage.
Representatives from Meta, TikTok and Snap voiced similar concerns.
They warned the bill could chill online communications because regulators would have broad discretion to determine what content or conduct is harmful.
The bill would also replace some existing mandatory industry codes.
Several people argued that this uncertainty creates a risk that platforms will over-moderate content to avoid large regulatory penalties.
The government has said a broad set of rules is the only way to ensure a safe internet.
The hearing continues.

Why did the Philippine economy grow slower than expected in the third quarter?
The Philippine economy grew by two point one percent in the July to September period, which was weighed down by weaker household and government spending and a contraction in agriculture.

Coordinated disturbances haunt grids worldwide. Here is how researchers solved the mystery.

Why are power grids around the world dropping frequency at the exact same second? Scientists found that internet-connected battery systems were checking their power levels at the same time.

Power grids rely on a steady frequency to move electricity safely. Grid frequency is the rhythm of electrical current flowing through grid lines. If frequency swings get too large, electrical equipment can suffer damage. Hydropower turbines are especially vulnerable to unchecked sags. Unbalanced frequency can even lead to widespread power blackouts. For years, mysterious electrical sags flummoxed grid managers around the world. Every sixty seconds, grid frequency dropped a tiny bit. These sags happened at the exact same time across different continents. Tennet Germany, a transmission system operator, brought the mystery to researcher Dirk Witthaut. Witthaut works at Forschungszentrum Jülich in Germany. Historically, hydropower plants drove low-frequency swings when water turbines vibrated. So Witthaut's team first tested a computer model of a Scandinavian hydropower plant. Turbine vibrations usually come and go over time. But this mystery frequency sag persisted every single minute without fail.

The researchers realized that such clockwork timing required an actual clock. They shifted focus from water turbines to digital devices connected to the internet.

The team installed over eighty power meters across their German campus. The meters sampled attributes like frequency and voltage once every three seconds. They measured distribution lines, solar panels, and battery storage systems. Meters attached to a battery storage system showed a drop every minute. Large batteries check their state of charge every sixty seconds. Since these battery devices connect to the internet, their clocks stay perfectly synchronized. One device checking its charge causes an imperceptible grid disturbance. But when millions check together, the combined drop becomes visible. In Ireland, data centers consumed eighteen percent of grid power by twenty twenty-two. Grid data showed Ireland's minute drop was three milli-Hertz in twenty sixteen. By twenty twenty-one, that drop quadrupled to twelve milli-Hertz. Recent sags in Ireland have even exceeded twenty milli-Hertz. The team also detected fluctuations in smart ovens and computer clusters. A recent study found less than three percent of smart devices run updated firmware.

More data centers, grid batteries, and smart devices connect to power grids every day.

Ireland's grid withstands swings of plus or minus two hundred milli-Hertz. Operators prefer limiting swings to one hundred milli-Hertz. A twenty milli-Hertz drop will not crash the grid alone. But if other loads sag the grid, extra battery bumps could trigger blackouts. Researchers say manufacturers can easily fix this by randomizing checking schedules. Regulators may soon demand changes, but solving the issue requires global coordination.

Now, let us look at news from Pakistan.

A protective barrier recently failed at a major hydropower site in Pakistan. The collapse happened at the partially-constructed Tarbela Dam T-5 hydropower project. The failure of this protective barrier caused a flood water surge in the area.

Next, we turn to space exploration.

NASA has opened a new recruitment drive for upcoming space missions. The agency is looking for astronauts to live and work on the Moon. NASA needs these new recruits so human crews can return to the lunar surface. This push comes after being gone from the Moon for more than half a century.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Have you ever noticed how fast your thumb moves when watching short online video clips? If a video takes just three seconds to get to the point, your patience might run out. Even a very tiny setup can start to feel like an unskippable pre-roll ad. Short-form video feeds have mostly eliminated the simple concept of an introduction. Today, almost every video begins right in the middle of the action. Because every video starts mid-action, basic context starts to look like wasted time. The result of this trend is not just about having shorter attention spans. It has created a whole new demand for hyper-edited reality. We have started expecting real-world stories to cut straight to the main punchline. If a clip actually needs an intro, you have likely already swiped away from it. Our overall tolerance for any kind of setup has nearly vanished over time. Even brief clips have turned into real tests of human patience. It is worth taking a moment to reflect on how this changes our daily focus. When ten seconds feels long, we might struggle to listen to longer stories in real life. Real moments do not come hyper-edited, and they rarely skip straight to the punchline. Next time you catch yourself swiping, ask yourself one simple question. Are you missing out on good stories just because they take a few seconds to start?

Thank you for spending time with Sift In-Depth today. Until next time, take care and stay curious.
